article.title: Rust 1.100 Stabilizes the Never Type, the Core Allocator API and Cargo Dependency Cooldowns, Which Do Not Apply to cargo install
article.summary: Rust 1.100, released November 12, stabilizes the never type and Cargo's min-publish-age; an April test run flagged about 3,300 crates for the never-type change, and cargo install ignores the cooldown.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

The Rust project announced Rust 1.100.0 on November 12, 2026, according to the [Rust Blog](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/11/12/Rust-1.100.0/). The [release notes](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.100.0/RELEASES.md) carry the same date, and the [GitHub release](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/releases/tag/1.100.0) was published at 18:19 UTC that day. The blog post lists the never type, the core parts of the allocator API and several Cargo changes, including a minimum publish age for dependency resolution (a "dependency cooldown"), and says the never type took "10 years and 5 failed stabilization attempts".

On release day, the independent outlets the Herald could read were [LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/1107187/), which posted a short note naming the never type, parts of the allocator API and Cargo's unused-dependency reporting, and [Linuxiac](https://linuxiac.com/rust-1-100-stabilizes-never-type-after-a-decade-of-development/), which published a summary that restates the announcement. The most detailed independent account is a pre-release LWN article on the never type, discussed below.

## The never type and its breaking change

The never type, written `!`, can now be named anywhere, according to the [Rust Blog](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/11/12/Rust-1.100.0/); the blog gives `Result<_, !>` as something that was not allowed before. The release also makes the standard library's `Infallible` an alias for `!`. To allow that, the blog says, the project changed the "never type fallback" from `()` to `!` in the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, as the 2024 edition already did. The blog says this "should largely be unnoticeable, but can affect code in some rare cases", and that the project issued compatibility warnings well ahead of time and released fixes to public crates.

[LWN.net](https://lwn.net/Articles/1091015/) described the cost in more detail in an article by Daroc Alden dated September 8, 2026. Its account, in date order:

- In April, LWN reports, the compiler contributor "waffle" ran Rust's crater tool, which builds public crates against a compiler change. LWN says 3,300 crates were negatively impacted and only seven were fully broken, the rest being broken through old versions of libraries that had since been fixed. The [crater analysis](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155499#issuecomment-4290467341), posted on the stabilization pull request on April 21 by WaffleLapkin, likewise says "There are only 7 failures" among crates broken directly.
- On April 23, reviewer jackh726 [wrote](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155499#issuecomment-4307446212) that there was "some concern about the amount of breakage in the crater run", that the sense was the breakage would be accepted "if we have to", and that the next steps were to look for ways to reduce it.
- Backports of fixes to old library versions followed. LWN says several authors were willing, "some refused on the grounds that those old versions were past their end of life", and the successful backports addressed 1,553 of the failing crates. In the [sqlx issue tracker](https://github.com/launchbadge/sqlx/issues/4247), a reply from the user abonander on April 28 said "I don't have the bandwidth to maintain 3 different major versions that are up to 4 years old", and a later reply said "There's also nothing stopping them from using old versions of Rust."
- The stabilization pull request was [merged](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/155499) on August 24 (22:30 UTC, per GitHub) with the 1.100.0 milestone.

For users whose code breaks, LWN lists three options: stay on Rust 1.99, update to supported dependency versions that include a fix, or add explicit return types to affected calls. LWN concludes that "most users of Rust will probably not be affected at all". The 1.100.0 release notes list 20 entries under Compatibility Notes (the Herald's count), among them the `Infallible` alias and generalized `Box` impls that "may cause new type inference errors".

## Cargo's dependency cooldown

The [Rust Blog](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/11/12/Rust-1.100.0/) says Cargo's min-publish-age is opt-in through `.cargo/config.toml`; its example sets `global-min-publish-age = "3 days"`. Cargo then skips versions published more recently than that and reports what it held back. One update can override the check with `CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_PUBLISH_AGE=allow`. The blog states limits: the feature depends on the registry recording publication times, "Versions without a pubtime field in the index are never held back", and cooldowns are "not a complete defense on their own". An earlier Herald Analysis of [cooldown features in pnpm, pip, Bundler, Dependabot and GitHub's package firewall](/article/2026-10/24-dependency-cooldowns-spread-from-pnpm-and-pip-to-bundler-dependabot-and-githubs-package-firewall-while-critics-question-the-approach) did not cover Cargo.

One point differs between two places. The blog says "cargo install ignores the minimum publish age, for both the installed crate and its dependencies". The text of [RFC 3923](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3923-cargo-min-publish-age.html), read on November 13, says "cargo install is subject to min-publish-age and will not select pubtime-incompatible versions". A source explains the gap. The [stabilization pull request](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17335) says there was "some confusion over what was being stabilized due to edits that happened during the FCP that weren't noticed" and that the resolver configuration is defined as not affecting `cargo install`. In an August 12 [comment](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17335#issuecomment-5271605091) listing drifts from the RFC, the user weihanglo named this and the removal of the RFC's `registry.min-publish-age` key; on August 21, [answering a question](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17335#issuecomment-5370386909), the same user said that `cargo install` works as if the feature did not exist. The pull request was merged on August 28 (14:57 UTC).

## Other Cargo and library changes

The release notes list four Cargo entries. Besides the cooldown, they cover a new lints system with a `cargo::unused_dependencies` lint, a new layout for intermediate build artifacts, and a change to `cargo install`: it "now uses the existing lockfile in the `.crate` tarball by default" and `--locked` becomes a no-op, per the [release notes](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/1.100.0/RELEASES.md). The [pull request](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17388) for the lockfile change, merged September 11, says that previously building and testing a binary could use one set of dependency versions while installing it selected another, and that a package without a lockfile falls back to normal resolution. By the Herald's reading, the blog post does not mention that change.

On unused dependencies, the [Rust Blog](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/11/12/Rust-1.100.0/) says the lint is `warn` by default, appears only when every build target that may use a dependency is built, and does not cover dev-dependencies. On the build directory, the blog calls the change internal but says it "may break build processes and tests that had workarounds"; the release notes say "The layout is not a stable interface and is subject to change."

The blog says the allocator stabilization lets libraries use custom allocators with `Vec` and `Box` "currently", with more collections and pointer types still to come.

## What the sources do not say

- None of the cited sources gives a post-release count of crates broken by the never-type change. The figures above come from an April test run, before the August merge and before the backports LWN counts.
- The October 2 [Rust Blog post](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2026/10/02/demoting-i686-windows-targets-to-std-only/) said both `i686-pc-windows-msvc` and `i686-pc-windows-gnu` would lose host tools with Rust 1.100.0, as an earlier [Herald Briefing](/article/2026-10/06-rust-demotes-32-bit-windows-targets-i686-pc-windows-msvc-and-i686-pc-windows-gnu-to-std-only-starting-with-rust-1100) reported. The 1.100.0 release notes list only the `i686-pc-windows-gnu` change under Platform Support, and none of the cited sources says whether the msvc change shipped in this release.
- None of the cited sources measures whether cooldowns reduce incidents in Rust projects.
